messages.author: fbff4100433066b4
messages.subject: Reparameterization & Change of Variables
parts:
Hi all,

Can't wait to see some of you at STAN conference next weekend. Meanwhile I have another question that I have been too shy to ask because I don't know if it is too basic or even dumb. 

My question is: Can data participate in the Jacobian adjusted transformation of parameters? For example if d is data, and p and q are two sets of parameters. Can I do the following?

f(d, p) ~ foo(q)

Function f is nonlinear in d as well as p. Let's say, I am also able to compute a square Jacobian matrix J for p -> f(d, p) transformation. 

STAN documentation has a section 17.4 that briefly touches this issue with Vectors with Varying Bounds but participation of data in the example transformation is linear.

Regards,
Vishy

parts:
Hi Vishy,

First off, please don't feel shy to ask questions. If you have a question that seems too simple, please ask: if it's simple, we're able to answer quickly. It'll save you time and reinforce the answer to the person answering. If it's difficult, that's good -- you'll find out soon enough.

On Fri, Jan 13, 2017 at 10:19 AM, Vishv Jeet <vishv...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi all,

Can't wait to see some of you at STAN conference next weekend. Meanwhile I have another question that I have been too shy to ask because I don't know if it is too basic or even dumb. 

My question is: Can data participate in the Jacobian adjusted transformation of parameters? For example if d is data, and p and q are two sets of parameters. Can I do the following?

f(d, p) ~ foo(q)

Function f is nonlinear in d as well as p. Let's say, I am also able to compute a square Jacobian matrix J for p -> f(d, p) transformation.

Yes: data can participate in the transformation and you will have to account for it in the log determinant of the Jacobian. Let me know if you need an example. But remember, terms that only include data and not parameters can be dropped -- they're constants with respect to the overall joint log probability distribution.

STAN documentation has a section 17.4 that briefly touches this issue with Vectors with Varying Bounds but participation of data in the example transformation is linear.

Regards,
Vishy

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reparameterization & Change of Variables
parts:
Look at the manual chapter on transforms.
In the simplest case, the lower-bound transform
can depend on data. But it drops out because
it's constant on the log scale. You can see this
in the math written out there. Basicaly, the data
shows up as a term, but if after you compute the
log Jacobian, you can drop additive constants.

The bigger question is why are you putting a distribution
on a function of parameters? Usually we want to think
generatively and only wind up doing something like you suggest
if there's an underlying generative model that we transform
for some computational advantage, such as a non-centered
reparameterization of hierarchical models.

- Bob

That's a tricky business in both statistical and computational
terms, and it will make your model a lot harder for people
to understand.

The standard thing to do is put constraints on the parameters
through the prior alone. You can define the prior in terms of
transforms of the parameters, but then you need a Jacobian.

Agreed. I was reading Jim Savage's blog post today and came across this:

...A similar issue occurs when we have a combination of continuous and binary or categorical outcomes. This is where the magic of Stan really comes to the fore. We can build transformed parameters that combine known data and unknown parameters into a single object, and then specify the joint probability of that object...

https://modernstatisticalworkflow.blogspot.ug/2017/01/building-useful-models-for-industrysome.html
